Physics seeks shared laws of nature and uses them to explain particular processes.
As research advances, scientists connect many phenomena into an overall picture.
Events in the world are not isolated from one another: its rich variety of phenomena is connected.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
**The mechanical picture of the world** Newtonian mechanics gave scientists an impressive, orderly picture of the world.
In its account of Newton's ideas, the textbook says that the world consists of "solid, weighty, impenetrable, moving particles."
It also describes these particles as "absolutely solid. They are incomparably harder than the bodies made from them, so hard that they never wear out or break into smaller pieces."

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
Maxwell established fundamental laws describing electromagnetic fields.
These laws could not be derived from Newtonian mechanics alone, so fields had to become part of the physical picture.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
**The electromagnetic picture of the world** In the Newtonian model of gravity, bodies exert gravitational effects across empty space instantaneously, an example of action at a distance.
Electrodynamics changed how scientists understood electromagnetic interactions.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
A single electromagnetic force cannot explain every process.
This is not a proof that a more unified theory is impossible.
It shows that the existing picture is incomplete.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
**The common structure of matter** Bodies in the world are diverse, yet ordinary matter shares basic constituents.
Ordinary matter in celestial bodies and on Earth contains the same kinds of atoms.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
This is its statement about the unity of matter.
The specific properties and transformations of particles still require theoretical and experimental study.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
**The modern physical picture of the world** Nature's shared features are not limited to the constituents of matter.
They also appear in the common laws describing particle motion and interactions.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
From the universe and Earth to living organisms, atoms and nuclei, studying a system requires considering its relevant interactions.
The four interactions do not all dominate every process together.
Their importance depends on the system and its conditions.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
The discovery of quantum properties profoundly changed the classical physical picture.
Quantum physics, which describes microscopic particles, added new elements to our understanding of nature's shared laws.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
Quantum theory provides a common framework for describing microscopic particle motion, interactions and transformations.
This does not mean that it already explains every natural phenomenon.
Fully combining gravity with quantum theory remains an unsolved problem.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
Physics has found shared laws behind many natural phenomena, but the unified picture remains incomplete.
Why these different particles exist, and why they have particular masses, charges and other properties, still raises questions for research.
